title: Solving Your Problem for You Can Also Mean Taking It Away from You
deck: There is often only a step between solving the immediate problem and taking away someone’s chance to form their own judgment.
body: When someone encounters difficulty, we can easily begin looking for answers at once.
How should things be arranged, which option is better, whom should they contact next, how can the worst be avoided? If we happen to have experience, the answers may even be perfectly clear.
Helping someone solve a problem always seems a good thing.
But some problems are more than an obstacle waiting to be cleared away.

They also involve how someone understands their circumstances, weighs the costs, and makes trade-offs between directions none of which is perfect. The eventual outcome matters, certainly, but the process of forming a judgment belongs to their life as well.
When we solve the problem too quickly, we may take this part away with it.

At first, the other person has only come to tell you about their confusion. A few minutes later, a complete plan lies before them. You have listed the steps, arranged their order, anticipated the risks, and explained why the other choices are not reasonable enough.
There may be no obvious flaw in the plan.
Yet the other person still hesitates.
At this point, the helper often feels puzzled: hasn’t the problem already been solved?
Perhaps what has been settled is the matter at hand, but not their questions.

What they really need to face may not be “how can I get out of here fastest?” but “what kind of person am I willing to become?”, “which loss can I accept?”, or “do I still want to continue in the same direction?” More efficient arrangements alone cannot answer these questions.
Making the right choice for someone is not the same as helping them arrive at a choice of their own.
Sometimes we even take their failure to act as disrespect for our help. If the answer is already so clear, why won’t they do as advised?
But an answer truly becomes someone’s own only when it becomes part of their own reasoning.

Others can supply information, point out omissions, reveal contradictions, and say what they themselves would choose. But if someone else always takes the final step, what the person receives may only be a route they can obey, rather than a decision they can take responsibility for.
This does not mean that we have to work everything out for ourselves.

Technical problems can be handled by professionals, repetitive work can be given to someone better at it, and emergencies may leave no time for a full exploration of oneself. We can live together precisely because we can draw on one another’s knowledge and abilities.
The question is not whether someone does something for us, but what doing so takes away.
Someone who repairs a broken object for you has not thereby taken your life away. Someone who handles a formality while you are briefly confused may simply be easing your burden.

But if, whenever you face an important trade-off, another person swiftly takes over the problem, delivers a conclusion, and treats disagreement as irrational, then they have taken away more than the workload.
They have taken away your place in forming a judgment about this matter.
One kind of help is particularly prone to this change: the helper is better able to bear uncertainty than the person concerned.

When the other person hesitates, we grow anxious. We want things to take shape quickly, want them to stop going back and forth, and want our own worry to end. Deciding for them is often not only an attempt to relieve their pain, but also a way of easing our own unease.
So we mistake speed for help and certainty for an answer.
Real help sometimes needs to slow down.
It first asks: “What is hardest for you right now?”

Perhaps the other person lacks information, perhaps the ability to act, or perhaps they simply need someone to stay with them as they put conflicting wishes into words. Different gaps call for different kinds of help.

If information is missing, bring information; if strength is missing, take one small step together; if judgment is missing, help them see the choices rather than using their confusion to put your own choice in their place.
Good help does not necessarily reduce every difficulty.

Sometimes, on the contrary, it leaves certain difficulties to the person concerned. Not because the onlooker is indifferent, but because some burdens become part of someone’s experience only when they bear them themselves.

The consequences of a choice tell them what they value, what they have overlooked, and what they need to revise next time. If others remove every consequence in advance, they may be safer, yet find it hard to know what their own judgment actually means.

Of course, when a decision also passes serious consequences on to others, it is no longer simply “their own problem.” Those who share the burden have a right to join the discussion and to refuse to be assigned the task of picking up the pieces.
Respecting someone’s right to solve their own problems does not mean bearing the results for them without limit.
You can say: “This is your decision, but this part of the consequences is yours to take responsibility for.”
This sentence neither takes their problem away nor pushes the whole of it back onto them. It simply makes each person’s place in it clear.
When help has truly done its work, it often leaves a sign.

The other person has not merely received an answer. They see their circumstances more clearly than before, can explain why they have chosen as they have, and know how to reconsider their next step if things turn out differently.
Such help may not immediately make them right, but it makes them better able to keep going.
The best help does not turn someone’s life into a succession of difficult problems successfully handled by others.
It offers tools, light, and support when needed, while leaving the most important question in their hands:
“Is this a path I am willing to take?”
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
